10038641:
TESTIMONY OF ALICIA REA, ESQ. LD 931 - Ought to Pass
An Act to Amend the Law Allowing Incarcerated Pretrial or Presentence Individuals to Be Credited Time for Participation in
Voluntary Work Projects in a Jail
Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
March 24, 2025
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety, greetings. My name is Alicia Rea, and I am a policy fellow for the American Civil Liberties Union of Maine, a statewide organization committed to advancing and preserving civil liberties guaranteed by the Maine and U.S. Constitutions. On behalf of our members, I urge you to support LD 931.
Under current Maine law, post-conviction inmates receive time credit for voluntary public works projects. This bill expands that time credit to pretrial defendants who are being held while awaiting trial. Given that there is a backlog of pretrial defendants who are often detained for a period of months--which this Legislature is doing good work to try to solve--this is a commonsense expansion of time credit. Offering one day of time credit for every 16 hours volunteered by both post-conviction and pre-trial detainees could help expedite their movement through jails and potentially prevent them from being sent to the Maine State Prison, based on the amount of volunteer time credited.
We urge you to vote ought to pass.

Testimony of Rep. Dani 0'HaIloran introducing

LD 931, An Act to Amend the Law Allowing Incarcerated Pretrial or Presentence

Individuals to Be Credited Time for Participation in Voluntary Work Projects in a Jail

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety

Good morning Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and members of the Criminal Justice and
Public Safety Committee. My name is Dani O'Halloran, and I proudly represent District 20, which includes part of Brewer. Today, I am here to introduce LD 931, An Act to Amend the Law Allowing
Incarcerated Pretrial or Presentence Individuals to Be Credited Time for Participation in
Voluntary Work Projects in a Jail.

Maine's Sherriff Association brought this bill to my attention, hoping to find a way to improve the lives
of inmates in correctional facilities while also addressing the risk of overcrowding. If passed, this bill will allow pretrial or presentence inmates to volunteer in public works programs and receive credit for time served. Specifically, for every 16 hours of volunteering, one day will be deducted from their sentence. This bill not only helps reduce imnates' sentence but also provides them with valuable skills
for future employment after incarceration.

When this measure was first introduced in 2021, it was in reaction to the COVID-19 influenza and was
an attempt to mitigate the spread of the virus due to close corridors. Let's not wait until there is another
emergency to pass this bill.

Thank you for the opportunity to present this measure. If you have any questions, I would ask that you direct them to the experts testifying after me.

District 20: Brewer (part)

Re: Testimony of MCCA regarding LD 931, An Act to Amend the Law Allowing Incarcerated Pretrial or Presentence Individuals to Be Credited Time for Participation in Voluntary Work Projects in a Jail
Chair Beebe-Center, Chair Hasenfus, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety:
On behalf of the Maine County Commissioners Association, we appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony to this Committee in support of LD 931. This legislation is common sense and puts those in pre-trial detention on the same footing as those already sentenced regarding the opportunity for sentence reduction.
About MCCA. Briefly, the Maine County Commissioners Association was established in 1890 to assist Maine's county government in providing vital services to Maine citizens in a responsive, efficient, and credible manner. The Association is based in Augusta, represents all 16 of Maine's counties, and is governed by a board with representation from each participating county.
What does LD 931 do? Under current law, individuals who have been sentenced are permitted to participate in public works related projects or in the improvement of property owned by charitable organizations, with the possibility of earning sentence reductions. However, those detained pre-trial or pre-sentence do not have access to these opportunities. LD 931 seeks to rectify this disparity by allowing pre-trial or pre-sentence residents to voluntarily engage in such projects, earning up to one day removed from their sentence for every 16 hours of participation, provided they are subsequently sentenced on the charge for which they are detained. This approach ensures equitable treatment and recognizes the value of constructive activities during detention.
Discussion. With current judicial backlogs, individuals can be detained pre-trial for extended periods of time (months), which in turn may lead to negative impacts on their employment, housing, and family stability. Allowing these individuals to participate in public service work not only mitigates the adverse effects of prolonged detention but also facilitates their reintegration into society. Engagement in such programs can reduce idleness, promote skill development, and enhance self-worth among jail residents.

Testimony of MCCA re LD 931 March 24, 2025 Page 2
A critical safeguard within LD 931 is the requirement for the sheriff's approval before a pre-trial resident can participate in a work program. This provision ensures that only those individuals deemed suitable and posing no risk to public safety are allowed to engage in these activities. The sheriff's oversight maintains the integrity of the program while offering residents the opportunity to contribute positively to the community.
There is also a financial benefit to the public associated with a program of this nature. Since nearly 90% of all county jail residents are pre-trial, a program that offers the opportunity to reduce jail time means less burden on jails and less burden on county finances. This benefit flows through to local property taxpayers who currently fund nearly 80% of the cost of operating county jails.
Conclusion. We believe that LD 931 represents sound policy by providing pretrial and presentence residents with the opportunity to engage in meaningful work, thereby promoting fairness, reducing recidivism, and benefiting our communities. If you have questions or need additional information, please do not hesitate to let us know.
Respectfully submitted,

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the
Committee:
My name is Peter Lehman and I live in Thomaston. I am a formerly incarcerated citizen and a person in long-term recovery.* I am testifying in support of LD 931 on
behalf of the Maine Prisoner Advocacy Coalition whose goal is to promote
restorative practices in order to increase public safety and the health of our community.
We often say that the opposite of addiction is connection. We mean that people who
are meaningfully connected to their community, to things that mean something to
them, and to people and things that give meaning to their lives are less likely to seek escape into drugs and other addictions.
Those who are positively connected to their community are less likely to find
connections to addictions and to criminal behavior.
That's what this bill promotes: meaningful connection to the community. Engaging,
WITH others, in meaningful community activities, helping to build their
community, having meaningful activity. Everyone wins.
And there is no reason why promoting this connection can't begin on day one of incarceration. Even before sentencing. While waiting. If you have to be in jaiol, why
not use it?
One reward is time off their sentence, if they get one. The more important reward is
the opportunity for contribution and connection.
This is a good bill. It's a positive bill----building community and connections.
Please endorse it.

* In the interest of honesty and disclosure, a personal background statement is available on request.

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Committee:
My name is Sarah Johnson and I am a resident of Sanford. I am writing in support of LD 931, An Act to Amend the Law Allowing Incarcerated Pretrial or Presentence Individuals to Be Credited Time for Participation in Voluntary Work Projects in a Jail.
This bill has so many benefits, including reducing the prison and jail population and so the total cost of incarceration. Physical and mental health degrade quickly during the stressful time of pretrial and presentencing. The stress of uncertainty for yourself and your family can erode self worth and motivation. The opportunity to do volunteer work and to be recognized for your efforts with time credited is empowering and motivating. The work may also offer new skills, training and experiences of working on a team. Motivational programs like this foster positive engagement and so will make the environment safer for everyone, including officers and staff. Who among us does not feel better on all levels when we have a sense of purpose? Legislation should be about public safety, supporting communities and improving the quality of life for individuals and families. LD931 does all that.
I hope you will support this bill.
Thank you for your time and consideration. Sarah Johnson Sanford, Maine.

TESTIMONY OF
SHERIFF TROY MORTON
MAINE SHERIFFS ASSOCIATION
ED 9�1 - An Act to Amend the Law Allowing Incarcerated Pretrial or Presentence In ividuals to Be Credited Time for Participation in Voluntary Work Projects in a Jail
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and honorable members of the Joint Standing
Committee of Criminal Justice and Public Safety. My name is Sheriff Troy Morton. I am the
Scheriff of Penobscot County and I have the privilege of serving as Vice-President of the Maine
Sheriffs Association and I am here today on their behalf.
Your Maine Sheriffs have taken the position of SUPPORT for LD 931 - An Act to Amend the
Law Allowing Incarcerated Pretrial or Presentence Individuals to Be Credited Time for Participation in Voluntary Work Projects in a Jail
During the 130"` legislative session, Maine Sheriffs introduced LD 419, titled "An Act Regarding
Participation in Public Works Projects by Pretrial Imnates." The bill garnered unanimous support and was successfully passed into law. Although the intent behind the bill was well-received, specific language regarding earned time was not included in the correct sub-section. This current bill seeks to amend and clarify that language for better implementation.
In Maine, approximately 85% of individuals in county jails are held under pretrial statutes.
Offering productive programming to incarcerated individuals is a beneficial approach. A recent
media report on a county jail's kitchen program highlighted several key benefits expressed by participants. They noted that engaging in constructive activities contributed positively to their mental health, fostered a sense of normalcy during their incarceration, and equipped them with
valuable, usable skills for the future.
In order to facilitate the calculation and application of additional earned time for sentences that
may be imposed, it is necessary to amend the language in Title 30-A � 1606 -- 1 -- B. The
proposed amendment would establish a prorated rate whereby one day would be deducted from a
sentence for every sixteen hours of participation in a designated project. It's important to note that this earned time would exclusively pertain to county jail sentences.
Your Maine Sheriffs urge you to support this amendment. I am happy to answer any questions you may have now or during the work session.
